title: Not numb
hook: how to hold the world's suffering, war and hunger, without going numb

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job's friends got it wrong: pain is not proof of failure. Your line was I tell you, nay. Did one shaming story loosen its grip? Today, pain that belongs to strangers far away. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

Eleven at night. A phone lights up on the nightstand. A headline about a war. Under it, a photo of a line of people waiting for bread. A thumb hovers for a second. Then it keeps moving: a recipe, a joke, a friend's new haircut. Nobody in that moment is cruel. The heart has simply been asked to hold more than one heart can hold, and it closes the door a little. That closing has a name in everyday speech: going numb. Today, two old voices on how to keep the door open without being flattened by what comes through.
screen: `A HEADLINE AT ELEVEN AT NIGHT.` → `THE THUMB KEEPS MOVING.` → `THE DOOR CLOSES A LITTLE.`

segments.voice: First, the Chinese teacher Mencius. In one passage he asks his listeners to imagine a person who suddenly sees a small child about to fall into a well. Anyone, he says, would feel a jolt of alarm and pity. Not to win the parents' favor, not to be praised, not because the child's crying is annoying. Just that jolt. Mencius calls that feeling a beginning of kindness, and some readers picture it as a sprout, the first shoot of a plant. A sprout is small, and it can be trampled. It can also be tended. Second, what numbness is. Read with Mencius in mind, it isn't proof that someone has no heart. It can be a sprout that got too much weather at once. The feeling doesn't die; it goes under, because it had nowhere to go. Third, a voice from Jewish tradition. In the Mishnah, in the collection called the Sayings of the Fathers, Rabbi Tarfon says something like this: the work is not yours to finish, and you are not free to walk away from it. Two halves, both needed. The first half lifts the weight: no one person ends a war or a famine. The second half keeps the door open: walking away entirely isn't the answer either. Fourth, put the two together, each in its own place. Mencius says the feeling is a beginning. Tarfon says do your part without needing to complete the whole. The feeling stays alive when it is given one small thing to do. A gift, a letter, learning a place's name and where it is on the map. Not everything. One thing.
screen: `A CHILD AT THE EDGE OF A WELL.` · `NUMB IS A SPROUT UNDER TOO MUCH WEATHER.` · `NOT YOURS TO FINISH, NOT FREE TO LEAVE.` · `GIVE THE FEELING ONE THING TO DO.` · then, large: `NOT NUMB.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one place in the world where people are suffering now. Just one. Say its name quietly. Notice whatever comes: a jolt, a tiredness, nothing much at all. Any of it is fine. Then, without leaving the breath, choose one act for that place. A small gift. A message to someone who can help. Reading one honest account from there. If you pray, you can hold that place in prayer. Decide when you'll do it today. The bell holds the time.
Not numb: keeping the heart's first jolt alive by giving it one small thing to do, without needing to finish the whole work. Today's word.
Your line: a beginning of kindness. Today, give or act once for a pain far from you, and let that one act be enough for today. Day seven hundred forty-seven.

screen: `DAY 747 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ONE DAY AT A TIME.`

howItsDone: Some people keep a small, regular gift for one distant cause, so hard news has somewhere to go; others hold a named place in prayer, or write to someone in a position to help.

myth: Mencius says people feel alarm for the child because they want praise
he says the opposite: not for favor, not for praise. just the jolt itself.
Rabbi Tarfon's saying says the work is not yours to finish
and in the same breath: you are not free to walk away from it.
in Mencius, the feeling of pity is a finished virtue
he calls it a beginning, which some readers picture as a sprout that can be tended or trampled.

fork.setup: a headline about hunger far away. you feel the jolt, then the urge to scroll on. which response matches Rabbi Tarfon's saying?
options: fix all of it, or it doesn't count.
do one part, without needing to finish the whole.
look away until it feels easier.
fork.reveal: the work is not yours to finish, and you are not free to walk away from it. one act counts.

original.note: Chinese, from Mencius: the 'beginning' or sprout of a virtue. Legge's English puts it as 'principle'.

trapdoor: what you thought: going numb to the news means you've stopped caring.
what it means: the first jolt of pity is still there, overwhelmed; one small act keeps it alive.
what a scholar hears: Mencius 2A:6, the child and the well, pity as a 'beginning' (duan); beside Rabbi Tarfon in Pirkei Avot 2.

notes: Mencius 2A:6 paraphrased (not quoted); Legge 1861 renders 端 as 'principle'. Confirm the 'sprout/beginning' gloss is fair and that 'a famous passage' is acceptable wording.
Rabbi Tarfon's saying paraphrased; the mishnah's numbering is 2:15 or 2:16 depending on the edition. Confirm the citation.
'Numb is a sprout under too much weather' is the script's own image, framed as a reading 'with Mencius in mind', not attributed to Mencius.
Hook and teach avoid statistics on news exposure or compassion fatigue by design.
Original 端: confirm pinyin duān and the pronunciation guide.
Editor: cut 'famous' (unsourced superlative); the sprout image is now framed as a reading ('some readers picture it as a sprout'), since 2A:6 itself says 'beginning'; myth reveal matched.
Audit: teach's summary said 'Mencius says the feeling is a seed', contradicting the editor's own framing (2A:6 says 'beginning'; the sprout is a reader's image); now 'a beginning'.
